title: AC Leaking Water Inside the House: How to Fix It
metaDescription: Water dripping from your indoor AC unit or pooling near the furnace? It's almost always a clogged condensate drain line. Here's how to clear it.
symptom: Water drips from the indoor air handler/furnace area, pools on the floor nearby, or the AC shuts itself off unexpectedly.
partsNeeded: Distilled white vinegar or a condensate-line cleaning tablet

steps.heading: Understand what's causing it
steps.body: AC units remove humidity from the air as condensation, which normally drains out through a condensate line to the outside or a floor drain. A clogged line (algae/mold buildup is common) is by far the most frequent cause of indoor water leaks.

steps.heading: Find the condensate drain line
steps.body: It's usually a white PVC pipe running from the indoor unit to outside the house, or to a nearby drain/pump. Look for the point where it exits, and check if water is dripping there normally or not at all.

steps.heading: Check the drain pan for cracks
steps.body: If your system is accessible, look at the drain pan under the indoor coil for visible cracks or rust-through — a damaged pan leaks regardless of whether the line is clear, and needs replacing rather than clearing.

steps.heading: Clear the line with a wet/dry vacuum
steps.body: At the outdoor end of the drain line, attach a wet/dry shop vacuum (with a rag around the connection to seal it) and run it for 2-3 minutes to suck out the clog. You'll often see algae/sludge come through.

steps.heading: Flush the line
steps.body: Find the access point near the indoor unit (often a T-fitting with a cap), remove the cap, and pour a cup of distilled white vinegar down the line using a funnel. This helps break down algae buildup and slows future clogs.

steps.heading: Run the AC and confirm it drains properly
steps.body: Run the system for 20-30 minutes and check that condensation is draining normally at the outdoor exit point, with no new water appearing indoors.

whenToCallAPro: If the drain pan is cracked, if clearing the line doesn't stop the leak, or if you can't locate/access the condensate line safely, call an HVAC technician — a cracked pan needs replacement, and repeated indoor leaking can lead to real water damage if it's not fully resolved.
safetyWarnings: Turn off the AC system before working on the condensate line or drain pan to avoid it running while water is actively draining incorrectly.
Standing water near the furnace/air handler and its electrical connections is a shock hazard — dry the area before doing anything else.
